drug_class: Chelating agent and disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD)
purpose: Penicillamine is used to treat Wilson's disease, a condition where too much copper builds up in your body. It is also used for severe rheumatoid arthritis and to prevent kidney stones caused by a substance called cystine. It helps your body get rid of harmful substances or calms down an overactive immune system.
how_it_works: In Wilson's disease, penicillamine works like a magnet — it grabs onto excess copper in your body and helps your kidneys flush it out through your urine. In rheumatoid arthritis, it works by quieting down the immune system so it stops attacking your joints. Scientists don't fully understand every detail of how it helps arthritis, but it has been shown to reduce pain and swelling over time.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, changes in taste (food may taste different or metallic), mouth sores, skin rash, and protein in the urine. Some people notice their skin becomes more fragile or bruises easily.
warnings: This is a powerful medication with serious potential risks. It can affect your kidneys, bone marrow, and immune system, so you will need regular blood and urine tests. It should never be used if you are pregnant, as it can harm the baby. Tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual bruising, bleeding, fever, muscle weakness, or swelling. Do not take iron supplements or antacids at the same time without asking your doctor, as they can block the medication from working.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on what condition is being treated and is highly individualized. For Wilson's disease, adults typically start with 250 mg once daily and slowly increase up to 750–1500 mg per day in divided doses. For rheumatoid arthritis, it usually starts low at 125–250 mg per day and is slowly increased. Always take it on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on your lab results and how you respond.
